data.title: Erythema multiforme — viva
data.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Erythema multiforme** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define erythema multiforme (EM).**
- Acute, self-limited, often recurrent immune-mediated mucocutaneous reaction characterised by typical target lesions in an acral distribution, usually triggered by infection (most often HSV)
- EM minor (no or one mucosa mildly) and EM major (≥1 mucosa severely, more systemic upset); now considered separate from SJS/TEN

**Q2. Causes.**
- Infections (~90%): herpes simplex (commonest — HSV-1 > HSV-2, appears 3–14 days after herpes), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (children; mucosa-dominant — MIRM), others (hepatitis C, EBV, orf, histoplasmosis, COVID-19)
- Drugs (<10%): NSAIDs, sulphonamides, antiepileptics, antibiotics
- Others: vaccines, radiotherapy, IBD, idiopathic

**Q3. Describe a typical target lesion.**
- Round <3 cm with three distinct concentric zones and a well-defined border: central dusky/blistered or crusted disc, middle paler oedematous ring, outer erythematous ring
- Atypical raised target: only two zones, palpable, poorly defined edge (EM major)
- Atypical flat targets/purpuric macules with blisters = SJS/TEN pattern, not EM

**Q4. Distribution and mucosal features.**
- Symmetrical, acral — backs of hands, palms, forearms, feet, elbows, knees, face; spreads centripetally; Koebner phenomenon; lesions appear in crops over 3–5 days and are fixed for ≥7 days (unlike urticaria)
- Mucosa: lips (haemorrhagic crusts), buccal mucosa erosions; eyes and genitals in major

**Q5. Pathogenesis of HSV-associated EM.**
- HSV DNA fragments (polymerase gene, Pol) carried by CD34+ circulating cells to skin → expressed in keratinocytes → HSV-specific CD4 Th1 response with IFN-γ → cytotoxic damage
- HLA-DQ3 association in recurrent EM

**Q6. Histopathology.**
- Interface dermatitis with vacuolar change, scattered necrotic keratinocytes (more than in other interface dermatoses), lymphocyte exocytosis, papillary oedema; sub-epidermal bulla in severe lesions; normal basket-weave stratum corneum (acute process)

**Q7. Differential diagnosis.**
- Urticaria (transient wheals <24 h, no dusky centre — urticarial multiforme in children), SJS/TEN, fixed drug eruption (multiple), bullous pemphigoid (urticarial phase), Rowell syndrome (lupus + EM-like lesions with ANA, anti-Ro), Sweet syndrome, vasculitis, Kawasaki disease, serum sickness-like reaction, annular erythemas, polymorphic light eruption

**Q8. What is Rowell's syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Lupus erythematosus (usually SCLE/DLE) with EM-like lesions, speckled ANA, anti-Ro/La, positive rheumatoid factor, chilblains — criteria by Zeitouni

**Q9. Treatment.**
- Treat/remove trigger; symptomatic: antihistamines, topical steroids, oral antiseptic/anaesthetic mouthwashes and steroid gels for mucosa
- Severe mucosal: short course systemic steroids (controversial), ophthalmology care
- Recurrent HSV-associated EM: continuous suppressive acyclovir 400 mg twice daily (or valacyclovir 500 mg BD) for 6–12 months even if herpes not evident
- Refractory: dapsone, azathioprine, mycophenolate, thalidomide, apremilast, JAK inhibitors
- Mycoplasma: macrolide/doxycycline

**Q10. Classify annular/figurate erythemas (PYQ: list annular erythemas).**
- Erythema annulare centrifugum (trailing scale), erythema marginatum (rheumatic fever), erythema migrans (Lyme), erythema gyratum repens (wood-grain; malignancy), EM, urticaria, SCLE, granuloma annulare, tinea, sarcoid, Hansen's, necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma — 'migratory erythema')

**Q11. What is MIRM?**
- Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis — children/young adults; prominent mucositis (oral, ocular, genital) with few or no skin lesions; good prognosis with macrolides and supportive care

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- Self-limiting in 2–4 weeks without scarring; recurrences common in HSV-related EM; ocular sequelae rarely in major

## Quick spotter facts
- Typical three-zone acral targets after herpes labialis — EM minor
- Recurrent EM — suppressive acyclovir

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Erythema multiforme). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
